title: Ukrainians Embrace God but Shun Moscow Orthodoxy
content:
Polling suggests the war has made Ukrainians more religious. But a closer look at more than two decades of data suggests a more complex picture.

While 12 years of Russian aggression have strengthened religious commitment among a significant minority of Ukrainians, the relationship between religious faith, church affiliation, and national identity has changed dramatically.

The share of Ukrainians describing themselves as believers increased to 71% in 2010, from 58% in 2000, according to Razumkov Centre research. Between 2010 and 2020, the share remained around 70%, though it rose during periods of crisis, to 76% in 2014, for example, following Russia’s occupation of Crimea and the beginning of the war in Donbas. 

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, the share rose again to 74%, before falling to 70.5% in 2023 and 68% in 2024.

This pattern suggests war and acute social stress temporarily increased the number of people who identified as religious, but the increases did not necessarily become permanent. It has not been a straightforward wartime religious revival.
snippet: Polling suggests the war has made Ukrainians more religious. But a closer look at more than two decades of data suggests a more complex picture.
creator: Michael Newton

title: What Counts as Safe AI?
content:
AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and IBM now boast an addition to their AI safety and security credentials: ISO/IEC 42001 certifications.

The certificate confirms that the companies have established a process to identify and manage AI risks. Although it does not guarantee that OpenAI’s ChatGPT will always produce accurate answers, that Anthropic’s Claude cannot be misused, or that Alphabet’s Gemini is free from bias, it gives nervous corporate customers something valuable: evidence that an outside auditor has examined a company’s AI management and meets the standard.

That’s enough to turn ISO 42001 into AI’s first global trust mark.
snippet: AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and IBM now boast an addition to their AI safety and security credentials: ISO/IEC 42001 certifications.
creator: Anda Bologa

title: Panicked Putin Reaches for Nationalization Button
content:
Vladimir Putin has signed a decree allowing the state to seize refineries, telecom companies, and retail outlets if their owners fail to adequately protect against drone attacks. The threat of nationalization by a regime with a fondness for the Soviet era is generating fear among Russian businessmen and oligarchs.

According to the decree, almost every element of critical infrastructure, including private enterprises that are deemed crucial for the country’s security and the economy, can be “temporarily” taken into government ownership for an indefinite period.

Few doubt that the decision was a panicked response to recent Ukrainian drone attacks on oil facilities, which have caused a massive gasoline crisis, and on at least 21 warehouses belonging to Wildberries, a Russian version of Amazon, that have already killed at least 14 civilians and caused widespread fear.

title: NATO’s Missing Link: Shielding Vulnerable Infrastructure
content:
A new railway is not a strategic capability if it ends at a vulnerable bridge. A battery is not a reserve if it relies on the substation whose loss it is meant to bridge. A second data center is not redundancy if both sites share a fiber route, supplier, or control layer. Such assets do not necessarily create strategic capability.

Recent US intelligence assessments reportedly warn that Russia may test NATO’s resolve between next month and 2029. NATO must be sure that the civilian infrastructure its forces depend on will work under pressure.

At the 2025 Hague Summit, allies agreed that up to 1.5% of GDP (of the total defense spending pledge of 5%) may include key national infrastructure and resilience. NATO has since approved a €27bn ($32bn) plan for improved fuel storage and distribution, for example, while the European Commission estimates that electricity grids need more than €1.2 trillion by 2040.

title: European NATO: How to Attack Russia
content:
An ever-louder drumbeat of menace has been emerging from Western intelligence agencies, culminating in a warning this month that Russia may be preparing an attack on NATO.

The clock starts running next month, according to US intelligence sources cited in the Wall Street Journal, which said Kremlin action could take the form of anything from a cyberattack to a limited ground incursion designed to break NATO by demonstrating a failure of allied resolve.

As the US scholar Andrew Michta said: “I’ve been warning about this. The three months I just spent in Europe confirmed my concern. Time to wake up and act. If appeasement of Russia continues, Europe will find out the price the hard way.”

That’s partly an issue of political willpower. Europe must assume that it will have to fight alone. That means achieving unity among its 30 continental members. The risks have been underlined by the US struggle to impose itself on Iran since its February 28 attack. This may no longer be a matter of American choice; it may simply be unable to help given its commitments elsewhere.

title: Digital Silk Road Builds Big Balkan Shadow
content:
Since 2007 in Serbia and 2008 in Albania, Chinese telecom vendors — particularly Huawei — have expanded across the Balkans, deploying 3G and 4G telecommunications infrastructure, as well as Chinese-built surveillance networks.

But both countries, plus North Macedonia, also promised to limit Chinese 5G involvement.  The US and Europe consider Chinese telecom vendors a security risk. This May, the US Export-Import Bank approved financing this year for Telekom Srbija’s 5G rollout, contingent on the operator using US equipment.

Will the recent US move limit Chinese influence in the Western Balkans, a term invented by the European Union to describe the six Balkan countries in Southeast Europe seeking EU membership, work? My analysis suggests no. The countries will remain addicted to Chinese tech.

title: Ukraine’s Defense Industry: The Motor of Post-War Revival
content:
Defense production capacity in Ukraine is projected to hit $55bn this year, according to the National Security and Defense Council in Kyiv, compared to $1bn before 2022’s full-scale invasion. That’s close to a quarter of national GDP.

Given the need to stay heavily armed even if Russia agrees to a ceasefire, and given the global interest in Ukrainian weaponry, the industry is likely to dominate economic reconstruction. Arms and the technology now embedded inside them could play as big a part in the industry as they do in another “porcupine” country, Israel.

More than four years of war, in which low-cost drones, interceptors, and missiles have been developed, tested, and honed on the battlefield, have resulted in unparalleled technological advances. And Ukraine can expect to leverage them for a hefty markup when exported to the West, the Middle East, and elsewhere.

The shape of a defense-led recovery depends on whether Ukraine makes the right deals in Europe as it seeks to maximize the value of its expertise, according to Tamar Jacoby, director of the Progressive Policy Institute’s New Ukraine Project.

title: Ukraine: Fedorov’s Election Call Will Fail
content:
The dust was just settling after Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov’s dismissal and the appointment of Yevhenii Khmara as his replacement. Then came the 35-year-old’s extraordinary nine-minute YouTube intervention demanding fresh elections.

If Fedorov was aiming to grab the limelight, he succeeded. But he has not changed the political weather.

The outcome of Ukraine’s political crisis now feels remarkably predictable. Fedorov’s campaign will fail.

Speaking as someone who lives and travels in Ukraine, it is actually quite difficult to find a voter who does not want elections. After more than four years of full-scale war, people naturally hope for democratic renewal, accountability and eventually the opportunity to decide who leads the country into whatever comes next.

But it is even harder to find anyone thinking now is the time for a new vote.

Keep that distinction firmly in mind, because wanting elections and believing they can be held freely, fairly and safely in the middle of this war are two very different things. That’s what made Fedorov’s comments such a surprise; his call seemed badly misjudged.

title: Unbreakable Shield: Why Taiwan’s Chip Expertise Cannot Be Cloned
content:
As Taiwan became the predominant manufacturer of semiconductors, Western governments became frightened and moved to “de-risk” from the vulnerable island that China claims. Taiwan’s leading semiconductor manufacturer TSMC responded by building multi-billion dollar foundries in Arizona, Kyushu, and Dresden. 

But if the goal is to end dependence, the diversification drive is doomed. Taiwan’s semiconductor ecosystem extends far beyond wafer foundries. It includes advanced packaging, materials, substrates, and the dense network of suppliers — all of which remains anchored on the island. Taiwan is no longer a “one-trick pony”; it has become a multi-layer platform almost impossible to replicate.

Consider TSMC’s investment in Arizona. It includes leading-edge fabs producing cutting-edge chips. Yet trade reporting and industry sources note that the technologies required to “package” chips, such as Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate, remain in Taiwan. Packaging lines on the island are fully booked, with long lead times.

title: How AI-Driven Influence Operations Attack Ukraine
content:
When US military aid to Ukraine fell by 99% and Europe stepped into the breach in 2025, Russia’s influence machinery pivoted. Storm-1516, a network linked to the Internet Research Agency, had spent years spreading fabrications aimed at undermining international support for Ukraine. Now it set its sights on the Europeans picking up the tab.

Germany, suddenly Ukraine’s largest military donor at €9bn, and France, whose president had emerged as one of Kyiv’s leading champions, became the primary targets. According to a February 2026 NewsGuard investigation, Storm-1516 has published 34 false claims aimed at the two countries since January 2025, generating 274m views. The core message: Ukraine is bankrupting Europe, exhausting its citizens, and dragging the continent toward war.
